questions.question: When does async Python usually help most?
options: When code spends significant time waiting on I/O.
When code is dominated by CPU-heavy loops.
When you want to avoid writing tests.
When all logic is synchronous file writes.
questions.explanation: Async improves throughput by overlapping waiting time.

questions.question: What do you get when you call an async function without await?
options: The final return value immediately.
A coroutine object.
A SyntaxError.
A background thread automatically.
questions.explanation: Coroutines must be awaited or scheduled to run.

questions.question: Why is `time.sleep()` harmful inside async code?
options: It converts async functions to sync permanently.
It automatically cancels tasks.
It blocks the event loop and pauses all tasks.
It raises ImportError.
questions.explanation: Blocking calls stall cooperative task scheduling.

questions.question: What does `asyncio.gather()` primarily do?
options: Retries failed tasks automatically.
Creates OS processes for each coroutine.
Compiles coroutines to machine code.
Waits for multiple coroutines and collects their results.
questions.explanation: gather coordinates multiple awaitables in one await.

questions.question: What does the event loop coordinate?
options: Scheduling and resuming asynchronous tasks at await points.
Automatic database schema migration.
Python package dependency resolution.
CPU vectorization.
questions.explanation: The event loop is the scheduler for coroutine execution.

questions.question: What is the best short definition of concurrency vs parallelism?
options: They are identical terms.
Concurrency overlaps progress; parallelism runs work simultaneously on multiple compute resources.
Parallelism only applies to async code.
Concurrency requires multiple CPU cores.
questions.explanation: Concurrency is about structure and interleaving; parallelism is about simultaneous execution.

questions.question: Which scenario is a poor fit for async-only optimization?
options: A workload with frequent database waits.
Many HTTP calls to remote services.
A pure CPU-bound image processing loop.
Concurrent I/O with timeouts.
questions.explanation: CPU-bound work often needs multiprocessing/native optimization, not only async I/O scheduling.

questions.question: Why should cancellation behavior be designed explicitly?
options: Because cancellation removes need for error handling.
Because cancellation makes code run faster by default.
Because cancelled tasks are always retried automatically.
To avoid partial updates and leaked resources when tasks stop early.
questions.explanation: Cancellation is part of correctness, not only performance.
